Results demonstrate that the proposed approach improves solution accuracy compared to standard McCormick relaxation, achieves solution quality close to the nonlinear formulation, and maintains computational efficiency.

item.title: A heuristic for optimal coordination of autonomous vehicles: static problems
item.description: arXiv:2610.37275v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the coordination of autonomous vehicles at unsignalized intersections, where trajectory planning and crossing-order decisions are intrinsically coupled, thereby making their simultaneous optimization intractable in practice. To this end, we propose a heuristic based on a hierarchical structure consisting of a series of nonlinear programs (NLP) in the lower level, which optimizes trajectories of each vehicle for a given crossing order, and a high-level heuristic to design new crossing schedules that exploits sensitivity information from the lower-level NLPs. Extensive numerical simulations across a broad range of traffic scenarios demonstrate that our strategy achieves substantially improved scheduling with respect to first-in-first-out ordering while preserving computational tractability.

item.title: A heuristic for optimal coordination of autonomous vehicles: dynamic problems
item.description: arXiv:2610.37288v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The coordination of autonomous vehicles at unsignalized intersections requires deciding both the trajectories of the vehicles and their crossing order, with the additional difficulty that the set of vehicles to be coordinated changes as traffic flows through the intersection. Since the resulting mixed-integer optimal control problem is hard to solve online, we propose an arrival-triggered receding-horizon scheme built around a schedule-refinement heuristic: for a fixed crossing order, a single nonlinear program (NLP) optimizes all trajectories and crossing times, and the first-order sensitivities of the cost with respect to the vehicle schedule are used to select adjacent swaps that are likely to reduce the overall cost. Replanning is triggered only when a new vehicle arrives, the new vehicle is appended at the tail of the current crossing order, and a memory of evaluated swaps that persists across replanning steps avoids redundant computations. Simulations of traffic scenarios involving streams of a few hundred heterogeneous vehicles show that the proposed scheme recovers most of the optimality gap incurred by first-in-first-out scheduling.

item.title: Probabilistic Sequential Safety for Stochastic Dynamical Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.37311v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this letter, we investigate a notion of probabilistic safety for a stochastic dynamical system. Standard safety notions are based on the idea that an unsafe region of the state-space must be avoided at each instant. In contrast, we study a sequential safety notion which is based on avoiding a tuple of target regions of the state-space. The proposed safety notion is inspired by many practical systems, ranging from modeling jailbreak attacks in large language models (LLMs) to predicting hazardous chemical reactions. In solving the sequential safety problem, we solve a sequential reachability problem for a stochastic dynamical system.

item.title: A New Parametric Uncertainty Approach to Systems with Time-Varying Delay and Feedback Stabilization
item.description: arXiv:2610.37354v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Delay Differential Equations (DDEs) with an uncertain time-varying state delay are often modeled as a feedback interconnection of a nominal time-invariant system with a time-varying uncertainty operator. However, typical choices of uncertainty operators do not admit tight characterizations of input-output properties. In this paper, we propose a new representation of a DDE with time-varying delay system as a feedback interconnection of a nominal fixed delay DDE with a time-varying multiplicative parametric uncertainty operator, where the parameter is bounded in $L_\infty$ norms -- yielding an operator norm bound on the uncertainty. We then provide a modified uncertainty representation which uses the $L_2$ norm of the parameter to bound the operator norm of the uncertainty. Finally, we show that by representing the nominal system using Partial Integral Equations (PIEs), these characterizations of the uncertainty operator can be used for stability analysis or stabilizing feedback controller synthesis. The effectiveness of the approach is illustrated with simple numerical examples.

item.title: Joint Antenna Positioning and Pilot Power Allocation for Uplink Fluid Antenna-Aided Cell-Free Massive MIMO Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.37428v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper investigates joint fluid antenna (FA) position optimization and pilot power allocation for uplink cell-free massive MIMO networks supporting ultra-reliable low-latency communication (URLLC) traffic under pilot contamination. By continuously adjusting FA elements within a prescribed aperture, we adapt the spatial correlation structure to the varying propagation environment. We formulate a joint problem to minimize the average normalized mean-squared error (NMSE) subject to QoS constraints governed by finite blocklength and Markov-modulated Poisson process queueing analyses. To ensure tractability, we establish an analytical quadratic relationship between the NMSE and the effective signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio through eigenstructure alignment factors. This mapping translates complex latency requirements into explicit NMSE thresholds, maintaining a median absolute approximation error below 0.03 dB and less than 10% relative error for over 90% of practical-regime samples. Given the nonconvex nature of the formulation, we propose an alternating optimization framework. Antenna positions are iteratively updated via successive convex approximation using analytical gradients and closed-form Euclidean projections. Pilot powers are allocated through a block coordinate descent scheme that employs safeguarded Newton steps to guarantee monotonic convergence. Furthermore, we introduce an auto-calibrated regularization variant to navigate the Pareto frontier between estimation accuracy and energy consumption. Numerical results show the proposed positioning yields up to 22% NMSE improvement over fixed uniform arrays while operating 7-8x faster than particle swarm optimization. The power allocation achieves within 0.5% of the global optimum at over two orders of magnitude lower computational cost, providing up to 39% pilot energy reduction with negligible estimation penalty.

item.title: An Open-Source Hybrid Ray-Tracing and 3GPP Channel Simulator for Non-Terrestrial Network
item.description: arXiv:2610.37536v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper proposes a hybrid channel simulation framework that combines site-specific ray tracing (RT) with 3GPP-compliant statistical channel simulation for non-terrestrial networks (NTNs). The proposed approach uses RT to generate dominant propagation paths and augments them with statistically generated paths and subpaths to provide richer multipath realizations under practical simulation complexity. To provide a complete simulation framework, we integrate Sionna RT, 3GPP, and hybrid RT-3GPP simulators within a unified workflow. Simulation results based on key channel statistics and power delay profiles show that the proposed method preserves site-specific propagation characteristics while providing sufficiently rich multipath components, thereby addressing the complementary limitations of conventional RT-based and purely statistical NTN channel simulators. The developed simulator is also released as an open-source project to support reproducibility and further NTN research.

item.title: A heuristic for optimal coordination of autonomous vehicles: real-time algorithms
item.description: arXiv:2610.37632v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When coordinating connected and automated vehicles at an unsignalized intersection, the crossing order and the vehicle trajectories must be decided jointly. For a fixed crossing order, the problem can be formulated conveniently in a bi-level form where each vehicle solves its own optimal control problem, whose optimal value is a function of its entry and exit times, and a coordinator optimizes these times subject to precedence constraints. We compute the first and second order sensitivities of lower-level problems, which are required to solve the upper-level problem, by means of algorithmic differentiation using the real-time software package \texttt{acados}. This implementation exploits tailored algorithms to obtain a computationally efficient implementation of the optimal coordination algorithm. We validate our implementation in numerical simulations that demonstrate both real-time feasibility and effectiveness of our algorithm.

item.title: A 2-DOF MultiBody Track Joint for Race Car Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2610.36407v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: TrackJoint is a Modelica MultiBody component that turns a three-dimensional road surface into a joint with two degrees of freedom. The two joint coordinates are the distance travelled along a reference line and the sideways offset from that line. Together they give the position, orientation and angular velocity of a single frame_b connector. All road geometry reaches the joint as a small set of periodic piecewise-quintic splines, so one component can represent any circuit whose splines have been fitted beforehand. The road constraint is closed with d'Alembert's principle. The two generalized forces that belong to the joint coordinates are set to zero, so no Lagrange multipliers are needed. The joint is connected to a multibody race car in Dymola and the pair is exported as one FMI~3.0 FMU. The same FMU is then used for time-domain simulation and for CasADi/IPOPT minimum lap-time optimization, with no change to the model in between. This works because the joint keeps the arc-length coordinate as a real state and publishes its time derivative, which is the quantity that lets the problem be rewritten with distance We report results for minimum lap time simulations on the Singapore Formula~1 circuit.

item.title: A Singularity Avoiding Track Model for Race Car Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2610.36430v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A track fitting pipeline is presented that converts a measured racetrack point cloud into a closed, $C^4$ differentiable, three-dimensional surface model suitable for high-fidelity Modelica race-car optimization. The surface is a Monge patch, parametrised by a curvilinear arc-length coordinate measured along the minimum-curvature line (MCL) and a signed lateral offset, with a height polynomial of user-selectable degree capturing the cross-sectional elevation profile. The choice of MCL as the reference line is deliberate since anchoring the same surface on the geometric centre-line can cause adjacent normals to cross inside the drivable region on tight corners. The resulting non-injective parametrisation assigns multiple curvilinear addresses to the same three-dimensional point and returns invalid road geometry. The MCL is obtained from a quadratic program that minimises integrated curvature subject to track-boundary, periodicity, and jerk-regularisation constraints. By reducing total curvature while remaining within the track bounds, the MCL moves the region of parametrisation breakdown outside the drivable strip on all circuits studied, keeps the normal map injective across the full track width, and yields a more linear time-to-arc-length transformation for minimum lap-time problems. The fitted surface and the associated track widths are exported as periodic piecewise-quintic $C^4$ B-splines, solved as a nonlinear program.

item.title: Structure-Actuation Co-Design of All-Electric Heavy-Duty Robotic Manipulators
item.description: arXiv:2610.36996v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper presents a mixed discrete-continuous multiobjective bilevel framework for the structure-actuation co-design of all-electric heavy-duty robotic manipulators. The upper level optimizes manipulator geometry and actuation topology, while joint-specific lower-level searches construct feasible archives of discrete motor, gearbox, and screw configurations. A system-level coordinator selects actuator packages according to hardware mass, co-design cost, and loss-aware supply energy, and the resulting actuator masses are fed back to the robot model until a mass-consistent fixed point is obtained. Evaluation on a full-pose SE(3) benchmark with a 100-kg tool payload yields eight feasible nondominated designs, all satisfying the 12 prescribed poses. Actuator-mass coupling converges in three iterations for every reported design. A fixed-design ablation shows that one-pass sequential sizing changes hardware mass by up to 2.13%, co-design cost by 10.20%, and supply energy by 9.40% in magnitude. Payload screening further reveals increasing mass-cost-energy demand and changes in competitive mechanism topology with carried load.

item.title: A Bi-level Co-design Framework for Lunar Monoped with 2D Jump and Landing Control
item.description: arXiv:2610.37199v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Legged robots for lunar exploration must be designed for low gravity, where reduced contact forces and long flight phases make leg morphology and controller choice interdependent. We study this for a planar monoped in lunar gravity ($1.625$ m/s$^2$) using a bi-level co-design framework: a differential evolution outer loop searches over link lengths, and each candidate is evaluated on a vertical jump by either a quadratic program based task-space controller (QP-TSC) or a direct-collocation based trajectory optimization. The two controllers yield different optimal link lengths, and trajectory optimization outperforms the QP-TSC across most of the design space, with 17% lower Cost of Transport (COT) at their respective optima. We then extend to a 2D jump, where trajectory optimization with centroidal angular momentum regulation produces stable in-place and forward jumps, and an LQR controller absorbs impact and stabilizes the robot after touchdown. This is demonstrated on a baseline morphology with both links 0.3 m long.

item.title: Spiking Neuromorphic Control for Periodic Orbits Stabilization in Underactuated Robots: A Greedy Lyapunov-Based Approach
item.description: arXiv:2610.37310v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This work investigates the use of event-based spiking controllers, implemented as spiking neural networks, for trajectory tracking in underactuated robots. Specifically, we address the problem of stabilizing a prescribed periodic orbit. It is well known that, by applying the method of transverse linearization to the robot dynamics in a neighborhood of a periodic trajectory, the dynamics can be approximately described by a linear time-varying system with periodic coefficients (a periodic LTV system). The problem of orbital stabilization can therefore be reduced to stabilizing the trivial solution of this LTV system. We show that a previously proposed Lyapunov-based greedy design, originally developed for LTI systems, can also be extended to the corresponding linearized transverse dynamics, which take the form of a periodic LTV system. This enables the construction of a feedback controller for orbital stabilization of the robot. The effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated on the trajectory stabilization problem for the butterfly robot.

item.title: Electric-Field Induction Motor with Discrete Circuit Elements and Improved Rotor Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2610.37452v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Electric-field-based actuators and machines lead the design space at the nanoscale and in biological systems, while having the potential to be used in favorable macroscale applications which prioritize minimal mass, performance in a vacuum, or performance in high temperatures. Electric-field induction motors consist of a set of stator electrodes which induce opposite charges onto a movable rotor surface. In earlier work, rotor surfaces for electric-field induction motors have been made of single continuum materials, which are limited in possible resistivity, permittivity and circuitry characteristics. To enhance design freedom, we develop a rotor for electric-field-based machines which may be constructed out of discrete circuit components between a finite number of conductive vanes. Magnetic-field induction motors, which are common in machinery, often utilize ``deep bar'' rotors, consisting of conducting bars which decrease the rotor time constant with increasing frequency using the skin depth effect. We propose, analyze, design and demonstrate a macro-scale electric-field induction motor which uses circuitry on the rotor surface to emulate the ``deep bar'' design, providing improved torque over a wide range of speeds.

item.title: Computing GR(1) Assume-Guarantee Contracts
item.description: arXiv:2610.37534v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Assume-guarantee contracts provide a set of algebraic operations that enable the efficient compositional design and analysis of complex engineering systems. The explicit computation of these operations at component interfaces is currently supported only for some logics lacking a notion of time. This paper develops theory and algorithms to compute these operations when the contracts are expressed in the GR(1) modulo theory. The key challenge is the computation of two quantifier elimination problems for temporal formulas. We develop context-aided variable elimination procedures on GR(1)-modulo formulas, establish their soundness, characterize subproblem-wise optimal solutions within an admissible class of formulas, and use the procedures to compute contract operations, including composition and quotient. We implement the resulting framework in Pacti, automating compositional reasoning over GR(1) contracts. Finally, we demonstrate the framework on an automated emergency-braking case study, where we compute system-level contracts and expose compatibility conditions arising from the interaction of component specifications. Experiments on synthetic families show that the cost is governed by the number of eliminated variables and liveness conjuncts, and a comparison with exact automata-based elimination shows complementary scaling.

item.title: A Benchmark Library for Distributed Power System Analysis and Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2506.20819v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: DPLib is an open-source benchmark library created to support research and development in distributed power system analysis and optimization. Unlike centralized tools such as MATPOWER and PGLib, no general purpose, reproducible data library package currently exists for distributed power system studies. DPLib, available at \href{https://github.com/LSU-RAISE-LAB/DPLib.git}{GitHub}, fills this gap by providing 40 multi-region benchmark test cases ranging from 5 buses to 20758 buses, along with a graph-based partitioning toolkit that converts MATPOWER-compatible systems into distributed regional datasets. The toolkit generates standardized \texttt{.mat}, \texttt{.csv}, and \texttt{.m} files, regional MATPOWER version 2 cases, local and global bus mappings, generator and cost assignments, explicit inter-regional tie-line records, and bus-to-region partition maps. It supports unweighted, electrically weighted, and user-defined partitions, and is compared with METIS, KaFFPa, and an IPA-inspired baseline. DPLib also provides ADMM-based distributed DC and AC OPF solvers for validation. Numerical studies report partitioning sensitivity, centralized run times, distributed OPF iterations, run times, and optimality gaps. These results establish DPLib as a reproducible data layer for distributed power system research.

item.title: Control and Stability of a Multilevel Power System for a Future Distribution Network
item.description: arXiv:2601.06766v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The growing integration of renewable energy sources into distribution networks poses significant challenges to frequency and voltage stability due to their intermittent nature and low-inertia dynamics. This paper proposes a multilevel control framework for a future decarbonized power system, using energy storage systems as power buffers to mitigate frequency and voltage fluctuations. A nonlinear interconnected model is formulated to describe the multilevel aggregated dynamics of the distribution network. To reduce the operational complexity and communication overhead of the control system, a distributed linear quadratic regulator strategy is developed based on bottom-up information exchange, where each level implements local feedback control over a short time horizon. Local stability conditions are established for the open-loop nonlinear model, and the closed-loop stability is characterized by the Hurwitz property of the system matrix. Performance bounds are also derived to quantify the gap between the distributed and centralized control strategies.

item.title: Revisiting Certainty Equivalence: The Structural Coupling Between Estimation and Control in Underactuated Nonlinear Systems
item.description: arXiv:2607.07276v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The certainty equivalence (CE) principle underpins a wide range of control architectures by enabling the separation of estimation and control design. While this property holds for linear systems, its validity in nonlinear settings remains limited and often implicitly assumed. This paper revisits CE from a nonlinear perspective, showing that estimated states induce an intrinsic coupling between estimation and tracking dynamics. By analyzing the closed-loop system in tracking-error coordinates, we demonstrate that nonlinear state dependence gives rise to higher-order interaction terms during aggressive transients. Motivated by this limitation, we propose an estimation-aware (EA) control paradigm that incorporates estimation quality into the feedback law to isolate estimation-induced loops. The formulation remains filtering-agnostic while preserving general applicability to smooth, underactuated nonlinear systems. We derive analytical conditions guaranteeing bounded tracking under uncertainty, validating the framework under high-fidelity quadrotor flight simulation along complex 3D trajectories at speeds up to 57.6 km/h. Frequency-domain evaluations demonstrate that the EA law extends tracking bandwidth by 39% and improves stability margins by up to 55%, effectively mitigating severe cross-couplings to offer a robust alternative to classical CE-based designs.

item.title: Programmable Sequential Memory in Coupled Oscillator Networks
item.description: arXiv:2607.18439v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Hopfield network established that static memories can be stored as energy minima of an energy-based model. Real intelligent agents, however, must navigate sequences of memories rather than isolatedcsnapshots. Biological cortex addresses this through a separation of timescales, where fast synaptic dynamics encode individual states while slow neuromodulatory processes govern transitions between them. Inspired by this organization, we propose a sequential memory architecture that is fully continuous and admits exponential storage capacity. The architecture is programmable, since the transition structure is carried by a mechanism that is decoupled from the stored patterns, driven by the input context, and free to be chosen, optimized, or learned from data. Specifically, we construct an autonomous three-timescale dynamical system with three coupled layers. A fast Kuramoto layer stores phase patterns as exponentially stable phase-locked configurations, an intermediate recognition layer sets the dwell times, and a slow attention layer routes the transitions. We analyze the stability, dwell time, and capacity of the system, and we validate the dynamics through numerical simulations of sequential memory retrieval.

item.title: Smoothing the Ramp, Not the Peak: Scheduling-Induced Power Dynamics of LLM Inference and Their Grid-Scale Consequences
item.description: arXiv:2608.01250v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language model inference serving is a fast-growing electricity load whose power dynamics remain uncharacterized from a grid-planning perspective. Using real, measured GPU power traces, we show that chunked prefill scheduling, a latency-motivated technique already deployed by default in production LLM serving, is a controllable knob that regulates power ramp rate without touching peak power. Contrary to the intuitive hypothesis that splitting a long prompt's computation into smaller steps should flatten its power spike, peak power stays relatively the same while mean ramp rate falls substantially. Critically, this ramp-rate benefit is not a fixed property of the policy: it grows monotonically with system saturation, and we confirm this along two independent axes: concurrency and long-prompt request load (from near zero at low whale incidence to 39.6% at high whale fraction/size). We translate this single-GPU mechanism into an operational grid quantity, regulation-reserve procurement, posed and solved as a chance-constrained problem using a model-free bootstrap directly resampling real measured power traces. For independently operating servers, chunked prefill reduces the fast-ramping reserve requirement by an estimated 24% at heavy load (95% CIs within 13-34%) and 12% at moderate load, consistently across reliability levels from 95% to 99.9%. Repeated with 100 trials per policy on two-GPU tensor-parallel deployments, the reduction is about 36% for a dense 14B model and 10% for a sparse mixture-of-experts model. The benefit holds for ramps resolved at up to 2 s and persists at a reduced 16-20% when servers' load changes are synchronized. Together, these results identify a no-cost lever for fast-timescale demand shaping that is available today, whose benefit is largest when data centers run hottest.

item.title: Deep Behaviour Cloning of Model Predictive Control for Real-Time Operation of a Hydrogen-Diesel Dual-Fuel Engine
item.description: arXiv:2609.33795v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Hydrogen-diesel dual-fuel (H2DF) combustion engines offer a promising pathway for decarbonising hard-to-electrify transport sectors, yet their highly nonlinear dynamics and coupled process variables demand constraint-aware control strategies. Model Predictive Control (MPC) meets these requirements but requires an online optimisation in every combustion cycle, which limits deployment on low-cost embedded hardware. This paper trains a feedforward deep neural network (DNN) by behaviour cloning (BC) to imitate an MPC expert, using 86,000 engine cycles of demonstration data collected at 1500 min-1 on a modified Cummins QSB 4.5-litre hydrogen dual-fuel engine. Two variants, one with process feedback and one without, are validated experimentally. Both track unseen fast-transient load steps (3-8 bar indicated mean effective pressure, IMEP) with normalised root mean square error (NRMSE) values of 7.80% and 9.03% against the expert's 8.01%, while keeping mean NOx and particulate matter emissions at or below those of the expert. Inference takes 2 ms or less on a Raspberry Pi 400 (ARM Cortex-A72 at 2.2 GHz), including 1 ms communication latency, compared to up to 7 ms for the MPC expert, a 3.5x speedup. Open-loop profiling on a low-cost ESP32 microcontroller at 180 MHz gives 4.3 ms per inference, 4x faster than required for the 18 ms cycle window. Beyond the training range the cloned policy saturates its controls but exceeds the pressure-rise-rate limit. To the authors' knowledge, this is the first experimental BC controller for cycle-to-cycle combustion control of an internal combustion engine (ICE), trained from demonstrations recorded on the engine itself.

item.title: A model predictive control framework with robust stability guarantees under unbounded disturbances
item.description: arXiv:2207.10216v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: To address feasibility issues in model predictive control (MPC), most implementations relax state constraints by using slack variables and adding a penalty to the cost. We propose an alternative strategy: relaxing the initial state constraint with a penalty. Compared to state-of-the-art soft constrained MPC formulations, the proposed formulation has two key features: (i) input-to-state stability and bounds on the cumulative constraint violation for unbounded disturbances; (ii) close-to-optimal performance under nominal operating conditions. The idea is initially presented for open-loop asymptotically stable nonlinear systems by designing the penalty as a Lyapunov function, but we also show how to relax this condition to: i) Lyapunov stable systems; ii) stabilizable systems; and iii) utilizing an implicit characterization of the Lyapunov function. In the special case of linear systems, the proposed MPC formulation reduces to a quadratic program, and the offline design and online computational complexity are only marginally increased compared to a nominal design. Numerical examples demonstrate benefits compared to state-of-the-art soft-constrained MPC formulations.

item.title: Perturbed Gradient Descent Algorithms are Small-Disturbance Input-to-State Stable
item.description: arXiv:2507.02131v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This article investigates the robustness of gradient descent algorithms under perturbations. The concept of small-disturbance input-to-state stability (ISS) for discrete-time nonlinear dynamical systems is introduced, along with its Lyapunov characterization. The conventional linear Polyak-Lojasiewicz (PL) condition is then extended to a nonlinear version, and it is shown that the gradient descent algorithm is small-disturbance ISS provided the objective function satisfies the generalized nonlinear PL condition. This small-disturbance ISS property guarantees that the gradient descent algorithm converges to a small neighborhood of the optimum under sufficiently small perturbations. As a direct application of the developed framework, we demonstrate that the LQR cost satisfies the generalized nonlinear PL condition, thereby establishing that the policy gradient algorithm for LQR is small-disturbance ISS. Additionally, other popular policy gradient algorithms, including natural policy gradient and Gauss-Newton method, are also proven to be small-disturbance ISS.

item.title: Gradient-Free Neural Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability for Scalable Safety-Critical Control
item.description: arXiv:2609.14087v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability provides a principled framework for synthesizing safety certificates and robust controllers for safety-critical robotic systems. However, applying reachability analysis to high-dimensional nonlinear systems remains challenging: classical grid-based solvers suffer from the curse of dimensionality, continuous-time neural solvers require accurate spatial value gradients, and reinforcement-learning-based approaches often suffer from weak boundary anchoring and non-stationary adversarial policy optimization. We propose a discrete-time neural reachability framework for control-disturbance-affine systems that learns backward reachable tubes (BRTs) and backward reach-avoid tubes (BRATs) through Bellman-Isaacs value propagation. Our key idea is to combine equation-driven self-supervision with structured policy learning: rather than computing explicit PDE-gradients, we exploit the bang-bang structure of optimal safety interventions to construct approximate teacher actions from gradient-free value probes, converting adversarial actor learning into supervised policy learning. To stabilize long-horizon value propagation, we leverage the learned actor to train the value function backward from the terminal boundary using a windowed temporal curriculum, where each window is used as the boundary condition for the next window. Across benchmark problems up to 80 dimensions, our method learns accurate reachability value functions while improving stability over existing learning-based solvers. We further demonstrate observation-space scalability on F1-tenth racing with over 16,000-dimensional egocentric inputs. The learned safety filter generalizes zero-shot to unseen tracks and transfers to a physical RC car, achieving real-time robust collision avoidance.

item.title: Wasserstein approximation of measures via orthogonal frames: statistical and computational complexities
item.description: arXiv:2610.36581v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Dimension-reduction methods such as PCA identify a subspace capturing most of the variation in the data, but not a distinguished basis within it. Selecting a basis in which the samples are sparsely represented is a recurring task in unsupervised learning, addressed by methods in factor analysis, dictionary learning, and subspace clustering. We pose this task as Wasserstein approximation of the data distribution by measures supported on the axes of an orthogonal frame, which, in turn, reduces to a nonsmooth optimization problem over the orthogonal group $\mathrm{O}(d)$. We show that, under mild assumptions, both empirical risk minimizers and a locally initialized stochastic gradient method recover the population-optimal frame at the near-parametric rate $\widetilde{O}_d(n^{-1/2})$, where $n$ is the sample size. The main difficulty is that, although the population objective is smooth, the empirical objective is not-this mismatch precludes standard covering arguments. We overcome this issue by replacing Lipschitz continuity of the empirical gradient with a coarsely Lipschitz bound, a tool that may be of independent interest. Numerical experiments support our theoretical findings.

item.title: Is Your LLM Relay Serving What It Claims? A low-cost and high-power test for LLM Relay Auditing
item.description: arXiv:2610.37086v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Relay and reseller APIs have become a common way to access large language models (LLMs), yet users cannot directly verify whether they receive the models they request and pay for. This opacity motivates LLM relay auditing, but existing methods struggle to combine low cost, robustness to benign deployment changes, and statistically interpretable decisions under black-box access. To address these limitations, we propose distributional fingerprint auditing (DFA), a statistical method that requires only textual responses from suspect and trusted reference endpoints. DFA repeatedly queries semantically simple finite-choice probes and uses the resulting categorical response distributions to construct endpoint fingerprints. It compares the suspect and reference fingerprints probe by probe and aggregates the resulting evidence using the Cauchy combination test, yielding an approximate endpoint-level $p$-value for audit decisions at a prespecified nominal significance level. Using registered fingerprints of candidate models, a likelihood-based formulation further supports model attribution under full substitution and joint estimation of substitute identity and substitution ratio under constant-ratio mixed routing. Our benchmark includes 16 proprietary and open-weight LLMs from 10 model families. Across 240 ordered full-substitution pairs, DFA achieves high detection rates at a nominal significance level of $\alpha=0.05$, using five probes and 250 relay requests per audit with stored reference fingerprints. Configuration overrides can lead to rejection even when the served model remains unchanged, with effects varying across models and configurations. Simulations based on stored empirical fingerprints demonstrate accurate model attribution and estimate substitution ratios, with estimation error decreasing as the audit budget increases.

item.title: Cost-based variable selection for prediction models
item.description: arXiv:2610.37353v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Objective: Variable selection for clinical prediction models is commonly done on statistical grounds related to model fit. Statistical approaches ignore the cost of misclassifications and the harm of measuring a variable. We aim to develop a decision-analytic variable selection algorithm based on net benefit. Materials and Methods: The proposed algorithm selects the set of predictors by exhaustively comparing the net benefit of all combinations using cross validation, with an extension based on backward elimination for settings with many predictors. Variables are selected if the increased net benefit from better predictiveness exceeds the net benefit reduction from the harm of variable measurement. Harm includes financial expense, time, resource allocation, and patient burden. We illustrate the algorithm through a simulated example and three real case studies. We compare its performance to traditional backward elimination and LASSO. Results: Across the case studies, parsimonious models were generated that optimized clinical utility with minimal impact on discrimination and calibration. Penalizing predictors based on their cost ensured that expensive or burdensome variables were only selected if they offer sufficient clinical utility. The algorithm was implemented in the R package NBvarsel. Discussion: Decision-analytic variable selection allows prediction models to maximize patient benefit while minimizing unnecessary clinical burden and costs. Conclusion: Clinical utility should not be an afterthought reserved only for implementation. By integrating a harm-adjusted net benefit metric directly into the variable selection process, NBvarsel allows researchers to select only the variables that sufficiently improve clinical utility.

item.title: Agentic Distributional Regression: Conditional Density Estimation through Agent-Written Programs
item.description: arXiv:2610.37611v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this paper we propose a method for estimating conditional densities from an iid sample using a language-model agent. The agent writes the estimator as a short program that, for each covariate value, returns the estimated conditional distribution of the response. The program is built from a library of probability distributions, so the returned law can be a parametric distribution, a mixture or a multivariate factorization, with parameters given by explicit functions of the covariates. Since the number of operations and constants in the program is limited, the fitted conditional density is a formula that can be inspected and evaluated independently of the agent, while the choice of the model structure and of the fitting procedure is left to the agent. We call this approach agentic distributional regression (ADR). Treating the returned program as a random conditional density estimator, we derive a finite-sample error bound under explicit complexity and optimization assumptions, and an oracle inequality for selection using independent validation data. For a stably selected regular structure with sufficiently accurate fitting, we obtain asymptotic normality of the fitted constants. In simulation studies, on twelve real datasets and on a new dataset collected after the agents' training data, ADR with Claude Opus 5.5 has the best average performance among the methods considered.

item.title: Unifying Sparse Estimation of Precision and Covariance Matrices
item.description: arXiv:2403.12357v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Penalized maximum likelihood is a widely used approach to estimate a sparse precision or a sparse covariance matrix. A zero in the precision matrix encodes a conditional independence and a zero in the covariance matrix a marginal independence, and the two estimators have been developed separately, each with its own algorithm. We show that these two problems can be unified via a single reparametrization of the last column of either matrix. This reparametrization decouples the likelihood function for each problem to a one-dimensional minimization followed by a penalized multiple regression. Our approach applies to any penalty that is separable in the off-diagonal entries and linear on the diagonal. When the penalty is the $\ell_1$ norm, it unifies the graphical Lasso and the covariance graphical Lasso algorithms.

item.title: Two-sample comparison through additive tree models for density ratios
item.description: arXiv:2508.03059v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The ratio of two densities provides a direct characterization of their differences. We consider the two-sample comparison problem by estimating this ratio given i.i.d. observations from two distributions. To this end, we propose additive tree models for density ratio estimation along with efficient algorithms using a new loss function, the balancing loss. The loss allows tree-based models to be trained using several algorithms originally designed for supervised learning, such as forward-stagewise optimization and gradient boosting. Moreover, the balancing loss resembles an exponential family kernel, and it can serve as a pseudo-likelihood with conjugate priors. This property enables generalized Bayesian inference on the density ratio using backfitting samplers designed for Bayesian additive regression trees (BART). Our Bayesian strategy provides uncertainty quantification for the inferred density ratio, which is critical for applications involving high-dimensional and data-limited distributions with potentially substantial uncertainty. We further show connections of the balancing loss to the exponential loss in binary classification and to the variational form of f-divergence, particularly the squared Hellinger distance. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed boosting algorithms achieve high accuracy at low computational cost, and that the Bayesian additive tree is competitive in accuracy while additionally providing uncertainty quantification, which the compared estimators do not offer. Finally, we demonstrate its application to assessing the quality of generative models for microbiome compositional data.

item.title: New explanations and inference for least angle regression
item.description: arXiv:2602.02491v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Efron et al. (2004) introduced least angle regression (LAR) as an algorithm for linear predictions, intended as an alternative to forward selection with connections to penalized regression. However, LAR has remained somewhat of a "black box," where some basic behavioral properties of LAR output are not well understood, including an appropriate termination point for the algorithm. We provide a novel framework for inference with LAR, which also allows LAR to be understood from new perspectives with several newly developed mathematical properties. The LAR algorithm at a data level can viewed as estimating a population counterpart "path" that organizes a response mean along regressor variables which are ordered according to a decreasing series of population "correlation" parameters; such parameters are shown to have meaningful interpretations for explaining variable contributions whereby zero correlations denote unimportant variables. In the output of LAR, estimates of all non-zero population correlations turn out to have independent normal distributions for use in inference, while estimates of zero-valued population correlations have a certain non-normal joint distribution. These properties help to provide a formal rule for stopping the LAR algorithm. While the standard bootstrap for regression can fail for LAR, a modified bootstrap provides a practical and formally justified tool for interpreting the entrance of variables and quantifying uncertainty in estimation. The LAR inference method is studied through simulation and illustrated with data examples.

item.title: CCAaaS: An Orchestration Platform for High-Velocity Design, Development, and Deployment of Data Center Transports at Meta
item.description: arXiv:2610.33231v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Today, data center networks run multiple congestion control algorithms (CCAs), each tailored to distinct traffic characteristics, from latency-sensitive intra-region RPCs to high-throughput cross-region AI workloads. The rapid evolution of AI training and inference further accelerates this trend by continually introducing new traffic characteristics that demand new CCAs. This paper introduces CCA-as-a-Service (CCAaaS), our eBPF-based ecosystem for the rapid design, deployment, and operation of production-grade CCAs at hyperscale. We present (1) a modular BPF-TCP framework and general lessons for designing modular CCAs; (2) a deployment and orchestration layer that provides disruption-free CCA updates, along with best practices for managing a zoo of CCAs at scale; and (3) a lightweight observability tool for CCAs and a blueprint for scaling CCA observability. CCAaaS manages over 97% of our server-to-server traffic using three active eBPF-based CCAs; two of the five CCAs we have built have since been deprecated. We show that our eBPF-centric approach to CCAs development delivers the same application-level performance (retransmissions, bandwidth, and tail latency) as their native in-kernel counterparts, and that our custom CCAs add negligible CPU and memory cost over their eBPF baselines. In terms of realized benefits, the CCA built with CCAaaS significantly improved network, and application metrics, for example, one of our CCAs reduced P99 latency for cross-region services by up to 20X.

item.title: Concurrent Task Orchestration: Hierarchical Trusted Collaborator Group Formation for Constrained Resource Allocation
item.description: arXiv:2610.33295v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Effective collaboration among resource-constrained mobile intelligent machines, such as Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), is essential for the completion of complex tasks. However, concurrent task demands, limited distributed resources, and dynamic collaborator availabilities make it challenging to satisfy task-specific completion goals in diverse collaborative systems. To address these challenges simultaneously, we propose a new framework of trusted collaborator group formation and the supporting resource allocation strategy for concurrent task orchestration. Specifically, a collaborative task is decomposed into subtasks subject to dynamic resource availability and inter-subtask dependencies. A task utility model is developed for collaborator group evaluation support subtask allocation according to task completion goals and unified value-risk analysis. Based on this model, concurrent task orchestration is formulated as a long-term utility maximization problem under $\alpha$-fairness. To solve the problem efficiently, we develop a hierarchical matching strategy that first clusters tasks and collaborators into coarse-grained sets and subsequently performs fine-grained collaborator group formation and task allocation within matched sets. Task-specific trust is predicted through spatial-temporal Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and embedded into a fairness-aware Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) framework to continuously update the matching policies. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed strategy improves concurrent task completion performance by 22% over representative baselines under resource constraints.

item.title: Analytical Modeling of Latency and Energy Trade-offs in FiRa-Like BLE-UWB Ranging and Localization Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.33423v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate position and distance information provided by Ultra-Wideband (UWB) can enhance a wide range of applications. However, its receive-mode power consumption makes continuous channel monitoring impractical for energy-constrained devices. Consequently, UWB systems often rely on Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) to discover peers and establish sessions before ranging begins. Although both technologies have been studied in isolation, an framework capturing the latency and energy consumption of the complete workflow is still lacking. To address this gap, we develop a unified analytical model for BLE-assisted UWB systems, from device-to-device ranging to infrastructure-based localization. The model includes closed-form expressions for discovery, parameter exchange, and ranging, and evaluates the resulting latency and energy consumption. Evaluation of three representative BLE configurations shows that the scanner consumes 28-57x more energy per discovery than the advertiser. In addition, the 99th-percentile discovery latency is 2-3.4x higher than the mean and reaches up to 110 s in the lowest-power configuration. The one-time BLE setup overhead is amortized after 24-562 ranging rounds, depending on the discovery configuration. Overall, the analysis demonstrates that the BLE discovery phase can dominate both the latency and the energy budget during short UWB interactions, making discovery configuration as important as the ranging scheme.

item.title: Learning-Accelerated Joint AP/RIS Optimization for Low-Latency Indoor mmWave XR Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.33945v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper studies a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-assisted indoor architecture for extended reality (XR) applications, where multiple access points (APs) simultaneously serve multiple users over a shared frequency channel under a centralized AP controller. We formulate a non-convex sum-rate maximization problem with coupled AP precoders and RIS phase shifts, and develop a centralized alternating optimization (AO) framework for joint design. We rigorously prove that the proposed AO guarantees monotonic improvement of the sum rate that converges to a coordinate-wise stationary point, despite the non-convexity of the resulting subproblems. Although AO provides reliable performance, its iterative nature limits real-time applicability as the system dimension grows. To overcome this limitation, we propose a supervised learning-assisted approach that leverages AO-generated solutions to significantly accelerate convergence. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves near-optimal performance with substantially fewer AO iterations, which makes it well-suited for latency-critical RIS-assisted XR deployments.

item.title: Kinetic Handover Modeling in Nonstationary Cellular Networks with Fluid Spatiotemporal Stochastic Geometry
item.description: arXiv:2610.34211v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Inferring directional handover traffic from aggregate mobility observations remains challenging because population density evolution does not fully describe the movement of individual users across cell boundaries. This paper develops a kinetic framework for geometry-induced serving-region crossings in nonstationary cellular networks, connecting boundary-normal velocity statistics with fluid spatiotemporal stochastic geometry (F-STSG) for density-based transport reconstruction. The framework distinguishes signed net population transfer from gross bidirectional crossings and reveals two information limits: density evolution does not uniquely determine physical pairwise transport, while first-order transport alone cannot resolve counter-moving crossings. We establish exact recovery conditions for potential transport and develop coherent and Gaussian mobility closures for estimating directional crossing rates. Sharp moment-constrained bounds further characterize the remaining uncertainty under bounded normal velocities without assuming a specific velocity distribution. An error bound links directional estimation accuracy to transport reconstruction and unresolved mobility information. The formulation also recovers the classical stationary Poisson--Voronoi handover law. Numerical experiments examine the information limits, reconstruction sensitivity, and closure accuracy. On 47 held-out vehicular simulation windows, F-STSG achieves lower net-flow reconstruction errors than three baselines, while auxiliary velocity statistics improve directional estimates under matched Gaussian mobility.

item.title: 6G Reasoning Agent Societies: Composition, Scaling, and Consistency-Time Laws
item.description: arXiv:2610.34357v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Emerging 6G control planes would compose Large Language Model (LLM) agents that exchange interpreted conclusions, so hallucinations can propagate even over error-free transport. Recent architectures audit each message locally against the sender's observation mask, but isolated audits miss collective behavior. Modeling the agent society as a cellular sheaf, we establish three laws valid on arbitrary topologies. First, the \emph{composition law}: network-wide divergence exceeds the sum of per-agent audit scores by exactly their hidden total correlation. This blind spot masks up to 23\% of joint divergence and, because the declared signal cancels in the cognitive signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), overstates it by $1.14$\,dB purely through topology; the resulting trust inflation preserves valid consensus states but slows convergence. Second, the \emph{scaling law}: reconciliation decouples across metric counters, so the worst-connected dimension sets the pace. Consistency time grows for a society size $n$ as $\Omega(n^{2/d})$ on polynomial-growth topologies of degree $d$, and paths breach a $1$\,s near-real-time budget at $n^\ast=13$ agents, whereas expanders ($\Theta(1)$) and radius-3 local audits ($O(1)$, $\approx300$\,ms) stay bounded. Third, the \emph{consistency-time law}: the timing error from omitted correlations is one-sided and capped by the worst-measured link. These laws, validated on simulated topologies and deployed LLM societies, give provable worst-case latency ceilings for near-real-time operation.

item.title: LunarRF: A Terrain-Aware Propagation Engine and Pole-Wide 3GPP Surface Coverage Atlas of the Lunar South Pole
item.description: arXiv:2610.34554v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Artemis surface operations will depend on 3GPP cellular links, yet no public product shows where such links are physically possible across the lunar south pole. We present LunarRF, a GPU system for terrain-aware surface coverage, and the pole-wide atlas produced with it. A footprint engine casts 8192 radial profiles from one of 11,827 candidate masts enumerated by stated rules on the orbit-adjusted LOLA elevation model, takes the viewshed, and evaluates ITU-R P.1812 Delta-Bullington propagation on every profile, continuous through the radio horizon. An order-independent resolver merges the footprints per 20 m cell, making the run shardable and resumable. The atlas covers the disc south of 80{\deg}S at 20 m for four SFCG-recommended surface bands and the IM-2 demonstration band, 1.8 to 25.375 GHz, under a stated link budget, storing per cell the best-server power and identity, redundancy count, line of sight and coverability. The engine is validated against a parabolic-equation solver, ray tracing and analytic solutions. Swapping Deygout for Delta-Bullington, or adding terrain noise at the level of the published height-error map of the DEM, moves the coverable class on under 1% of a mast's disc in the mean. With every candidate active, 90.5% of the disc is coverable at 1.8 GHz, 59% at 5.855 GHz and 10% at 25.375 GHz, or 84, 43 and 5% after the measured 3-4 dB engine optimism. A mast covers about 90% of its visible area within its budget-set range, and no band is terrain-limited. The nine current Artemis regions are 85-99% coverable at 1.8 GHz and 22-85% at 5.855 GHz. The atlas and candidate table are released with a DOI.

item.title: Denial of Service Attacks on Beam Allocation in Large LEO Constellations
item.description: arXiv:2610.34631v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the vulnerability of beam allocation approaches in large low-Earth-orbit (LEO) satellite constellations to adversarial demand inflation resulting in denial-of-service attacks. We consider an attack model in which an adversary places (injects) additional terminals and evaluate these attacks against greedy and max-min-fair beam allocation algorithms, each combined with either equal or demand-proportional intra-cell capacity sharing. Vulnerability is measured using mean demand satisfaction, coverage, and the fraction of legitimate users receiving at least a threshold fraction of their requested capacity under several attack heuristics. There is a trade-off for the system between robustness and performance, meaning the algorithm with the most vulnerability to the attacks (greedy-proportional) has the highest performance before the attacks. Demand-proportional sharing increases the fraction of under-served users up to 34% under both allocation algorithms, whereas equal sharing limits the increase up to 13%. The sharing rule also changes the most damaging attack allocation in nearly all cases: demand-proportional sharing rewards concentrating injected terminals in the most loaded cells, while equal sharing performs better when distributing these terminals across the least loaded cells. Furthermore, the max-min-fair beam allocation algorithm forces the attacker to use a higher number of targeted cells to result in extensive damage to the system.

item.title: Satellite Intelligence: Distributed Training, Collaborative Inference,and LLM Adaptation in LEO Constellation
item.description: arXiv:2610.35282v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The proliferation of orbital sensing data and the real-time demands of emerging global services are pushing low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite networks from bent-pipe relays toward intelligent onboard processing. This shift confronts a fundamental tension, where modern artificial intelligence (AI) training paradigms require intensive computation, abundant memory, and stable connectivity, all of which are scarce under the dynamic topologies, intermittent links, and severe size, weight, and power (SWaP) constraints of satellite networks. Addressing this tension demands rethinking AI workflows, from training and inference to the emerging deployment of large language models (LLMs), under a constraint-aware design philosophy. To the best of our knowledge, this paper provides the first survey that jointly covers all three, whereas prior surveys examine these aspects in isolation. We begin by identifying the deployment challenge of satellite intelligence (SI) and deriving design principles for SI. We then examine three advancing paradigms: i) distributed training, where federated learning (FL) and split learning (SL) enable satellite-ground co-training under resource limitations; ii) collaborative inference, which exploits single-satellite, multi-satellite, and satellite-ground architectures to meet real-time service demands; and iii) on-orbit LLM adaptation and serving, which tackles the frontier challenge of deploying LLMs under severe orbital constraints and resource-aware serving. Finally, we identify open challenges and future directions. By bridging the AI and satellite networks, this paper provides a research roadmap for the implementation of space-native AI technologies.

item.title: Trim: Fee Level Matters More Than Skew in Lightning Routing
item.description: arXiv:2610.35296v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Lightning routing nodes lend their channel balance for a posted fee. Operators' tools move that fee with the balance around a hand-set level, and which part of the fee drives revenue is unclear. We present Trim, which models a channel as a two-sided inventory with costly refills. Its optimal fee is a level, set by demand and replenishment, plus a balance skew, the shadow price of liquidity. The level is first order: no fee rule beats the ceiling demand and replenishment set, and on exactly solved channels the best flat fee comes within $1.6\%$ of the optimum at the median, whereas a level off by a factor of two loses tens of percent. The skew is second-order insurance: it adds at most what the flow-balancing flat fee loses to refused forwards. So the level should be chosen: Trim's rule traces the revenue--success frontier, posts one level on every channel, and adds a skew only where refills stay frequent and costly. On a 2026 snapshot with synthetic payments, no tuned tool beats that frontier by over a few percent, and a skew changes gross revenue by a few percent.

item.title: Uncertainty-Guided Counterfactual Sensor Selection and Safety-Gated Recognition for Autonomous Sensing Agents in IoT Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.35344v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous IoT systems rely on distributed sensing, but sensor faults and communication loss can leave multichannel evidence incomplete or unreliable. Their agents must therefore classify measurements, assess evidence sufficiency, select a sensor to reacquire, and hand off unsafe decisions. We formulate counterfactual sensing: a degraded window defines the factual state, each candidate restoration defines a controlled alternative, and a pre-request utility model estimates loss reduction. Physics-Guided Invariant-Kinematic Fusion (PGIK-Fusion) constructs class evidence, while calibrated risk and cost-sensitive utility select acceptance, sensor request, or handoff from factual information. On the Logistic Activity Recognition Challenge dataset, PGIK-Fusion achieves 0.768 accuracy and a macro-averaged F1 score (Macro-F1) of 0.696, exceeding extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost)--one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D-CNN) fusion by 2.49 and 2.00 percentage points, respectively. Across seven predefined degradation conditions on held-out subjects, the policy reduces unsafe acceptance from 33.0% to 13.8%; relative to an action-rate-matched random policy, it raises automation accuracy by 18.5 percentage points and lowers expected cost by 24.7%. In the auxiliary within-event wind-turbine study, PGIK-Fusion reaches 0.975 Macro-F1, improves on XGBoost--1D-CNN by 1.17 percentage points, and reduces unsafe acceptance from 20.1% to 8.0%. The evaluation characterizes the controlled responses of a frozen recognition model to specified sensor restorations under predefined fault families and severities. Within this scope, the results demonstrate that calibrated recognition, targeted evidence acquisition, and conservative deferral can form a unified perception--action loop that reduces unsafe automation under sensor degradation.

item.title: Routing Around the Queue: An Evaluation of Eco-Routing Protocol on different Traffic Scenarios
item.description: arXiv:2610.35479v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We evaluate ErouVe, a vehicular eco-routing protocol in which roadside units (RSUs) collect per-segment travel-time and CO2 reports from passing vehicles and answer route requests with the lowest-cost alternative, across a range of road architectures and traffic scenarios. We conduct the evaluation with a working implementation of the protocol inside Veins, adapted to drive SUMO's own router rather than a hand-rolled shortest-path search, on a network offering a short, signal-controlled route and a longer, signal-free bypass, under two traffic scenarios. This evaluation reveals clear strengths and weaknesses of the protocol. Under light, uncongested traffic, ErouVe's fleet-wide effect is light. Under traffic dense enough to stress the signalized route's throughput and produce a real, growing queue, the same protocol succeeds a medium fleet-wide CO2 reduction, with diverted vehicles individually saving even more fuels. We use these findings to propose three targeted corrective methods; a knowledge-gated cost-acceptance rule, a diversion-locking rule, and a distance-normalized CO2 cost function, that respectively address a cold-start knowledge asymmetry, decision flapping under noisy crowd-sourced data, and a per-second CO2 metric that rewards idling. Each of these weaknesses are generic pitfalls for any crowd-sourced routing signal and all proposed methods measurably restore protocol effectiveness.

item.title: RLNC vs Reed-Solomon in Satellite Channels: Crossover Analysis and the Bridging Property
item.description: arXiv:2610.35649v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Satellite communication systems are increasingly relied upon for connectivity in remote areas and are expected to play a pivotal role in 6G networks, operating under high round-trip times and packet loss where forward error correction is essential. This work evaluates Reed-Solomon (RS) coding, Random Linear Network Coding (RLNC), and a combined RS+RLNC hybrid over a three-hop satellite channel whose loss statistics are derived from orbital geometry and link-budget calculations rather than assumed, comparing RS and RLNC at matched code rates of 0.800. The central finding is the \emph{bridging property} of RLNC: every RS code rate collapses above a crossover threshold $p^*$, while RLNC operates continuously through all failure regions with overhead growing as $1/(1-p)$. At rate~0.800, $p^* \approx 0.21$. Under the derived satcom channel with mean burst duration 166~minutes, RS$(255,204)$ is impractical despite an average loss rate of 1%, while RLNC requires 15.5~Mbit to recover all 1000 packets. An RS+RLNC hybrid reduces overhead by 19% relative to pure RLNC at BER$=10^{-3}$. To the authors' knowledge, this is the first analytical derivation of the rate-normalised crossover $p^*$ between RS and RLNC and the first experimental confirmation of the bridging property under a physically derived satellite channel model.

item.title: Terra-Fi: Decoupling Sensing and Wireless Depths for Sustainable Deep Underground Monitoring
item.description: arXiv:2610.33202v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Wireless underground sensor networks (WUSNs) enable in-situ monitoring of subsurface processes and buried assets to deliver substantial social and economic benefits across diverse verticals. However, meter-scale underground monitoring remains challenging since conventional WUSNs place the entire underground device at the target sensing depth, where severe soil-induced attenuation significantly degrades communication reliability and makes wireless energy transfer (WET) inefficient and even impractical. To address this limitation, we propose Terra-Fi, a novel shallow-hub and deep-sensing architecture that decouples the sensing depth from the wireless communication and energy-replenishment depth. In Terra-Fi, a shallow wireless hub is deployed at a depth favorable for communication, WET, and maintenance, while application-specific sensing probes are extended to meter-scale target layers through power-and-signal feeders. On this basis, we first examine the depth limitations of underground communication and WET and compare representative monitoring architectures. Then, we present its system architecture, operation flow, and potential benefits. Through a precision agriculture case study, our numerical results reveal that Terra-Fi establishes more robust wireless connectivity and a longer operational lifetime than conventional fully buried WUSN architectures, particularly at greater sensing depths and higher volumetric water content. Moreover, its performance gain can be enhanced through time allocation and transmission-configuration optimization. Finally, we pinpoint practical challenges and future research directions for deploying Terra-Fi into WUSN systems.

item.title: Security evaluation of 6G-oriented and O-RAN networks through targeted attacks
item.description: arXiv:2610.33526v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The sixth generation (6G) of networks is supported by increased bandwidth, automation through the use of O-RAN technologies. Simultaneously though autonomous operation leads to an extensive threat surface and sophisticated attacks. Understanding the attack impact, the Tactics, Techniques and Procedures that are used by attackers is extremely challenging, but however is crucial for developing defense and mitigation strategies against them. This paper evaluates a targeted attack chain against a virtualized, 6G-oriented O-RAN testbed in which the F1 midhaul interface is accessible to an attacker and transport-layer protection is not enabled. The attack disrupts the legitimate O-DU association, introduces a rogue O-DU using observed configuration parameters, and intercepts user-plane traffic. The attack was evaluated in a fully virtualized testbed based on Open5GS, the srsRAN Project, FlexRIC, and an Electric Vehicle (EV) charging infrastructure based on OCPP 1.6.

item.title: Queuing for Inference: Dynamic Memory Footprints and Costly Preemption
item.description: arXiv:2610.33923v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Modeling inference workloads for transformer-based neural networks poses unique challenges due to their dynamic memory footprints, head-of-line blocking caused by heavy-tailed request distributions, and memory-dependent preemption overhead arising from the need to load/unload cache state. In this paper, we introduce a new queuing model that captures the impacts of these features on system stability and scheduling design. We show that the Gittins-index policy, which minimizes mean response time in the standard M/G/1 setting, can incur substantial preemption overhead in our model. Motivated by this limitation, we propose the Multi-Level-Priority-Threshold (MLPT) policy, that limits preemption while preserving priority for short jobs. We characterize the mean response time under MLPT and provide empirical rules-of-thumb to solve the resulting threshold-optimization problem. Our key observation is that optimal scheduling is a balance between reducing the response times of shorter jobs and limiting the overhead incurred when preemption occurs. These results provide a theoretical framework for understanding scheduling in memory constrained queuing systems for inference tasks.

item.title: Unifying Performance and Equity via Percentile Optimization and Cell-Free Massive MIMO
item.description: arXiv:2610.33982v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Improving the throughput of the weakest users is a central objective of wireless resource allocation, and the objective around which the user-centric cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (UC-mMIMO) architecture is built. This paper brings the two together by formulating and solving percentile programs for UC-mMIMO networks. We maximize the sum-least-qth-percentile (SLqP) rate via downlink power control, a utility that targets the user equipments (UEs) in the lowest q percentile of the rate distribution and subsumes max-min-rate and sum-rate maximization as special cases. The problem is non-convex, non-smooth and NP-hard. The cyclic maximization approach of one of the previous percentile optimization series does not carry over: the coherent joint transmission technique introduces cross terms in the powers that destroy the block-concavity on which it relies. We develop a change of variables that restores block-concavity, yielding an algorithm with closed-form auxiliary updates and a concave power update, and we give a self-contained proof of non-decreasing convergence to a directional stationary point. Simulations establish two facts: first, percentile optimization retains its value in an architecture with no cell edges; relative to the weighted minimum mean-square error benchmark, it raises the average rate of the lowest-10th-percentile UEs by 56--72% and Jain's fairness index from below 0.92 to above 0.99. Second, compared directly with massive MIMO and small cells under the same SLqP utility, UC-mMIMO delivers the highest lower-percentile rates at every access point density tested, by up to 62% and 2.7$\times$ respectively, at the same fairness, and its advantage widens with densification.

item.title: BE-CTDE: Blockchain-Enabled Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Anomaly Detection and Token Economics
item.description: arXiv:2610.34121v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning supports cooperative decision-making in Internet of Things systems, but strategic deviations can disrupt coordination and undermine confidence in the training process. This paper proposes Blockchain-Enabled Centralized Training and Decentralized Execution (BE-CTDE), which uses blockchain as an active training-management layer. A behavioral verifier compares executed trajectories with shared-policy recommendations; its flags drive a token mechanism combining slashing, burning, rewards, and compensation. Retained balances determine each agent's contribution to the global policy update, connecting auditable behavior to learning influence. We derive a one-round incentive condition that accounts for action-dependent compensation and the payoff from deviation, and a finite expected exclusion-time bound under explicit conditional detection and accounting assumptions, showing perfect detection is unnecessary. An exact finite-population capacity bound characterizes the limits of the population-relative detector. In multi-agent path finding experiments, BE-CTDE outperforms a state-of-the-art learning-based path planner with substantially higher success rates under attack, even when adversaries form the majority. It also outperforms partially defended baselines in all configurations, with collision rates up to 35% lower than under detection without economic consequences and up to 43% lower than under conventional stake slashing. Together, these results characterize how behavioral verification and token feedback can support accountable cooperative learning.

item.title: Networked Humanoid Intelligence: Communication, Coordination, Collaboration, and Social Interaction
item.description: arXiv:2610.34740v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Humanoid robots are moving from laboratory platforms toward connected fleets that share workspaces, infrastructure, tasks, and knowledge with other robots and humans. As deployments grow, the operation and improvement of each humanoid depend on information exchanged across the network. However, existing research has largely studied humanoids as individual systems. This survey examines networked humanoid intelligence through four functions of information exchange: communication, coordination, collaboration, and social intelligence with human interaction. We first establish the foundations of networked humanoid systems, define the question addressed by each function, and connect them through a common factory scenario. We review the literature along six dimensions: interaction architecture, exchanged information, physical coupling, operating timescale, system scale, and embodiment. We separate results obtained with physical and simulated humanoids from those based on other robotic platforms or disembodied agents, because the latter do not fully capture humanoid-specific constraints such as balance, whole-body motion, contact, and physical interaction. We examine hardware, datasets, and benchmarks, and distinguish risks handled locally from those networking introduces, such as stale information or unsafe knowledge propagation. Finally, we identify open problems in control-aware networking, compact body-centric messages, physically grounded coordination, network- and embodiment-aware knowledge sharing, fleet-level social consistency, and accountable human oversight.

item.title: HiLO: Towards Product-Level Graceful Degradation with a Quality-Aware, Load-Aware Control Framework
item.description: arXiv:2610.34844v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Graceful degradation is a key mechanism employed by large-scale systems to handle overload conditions. Its importance has grown further as GPU-intensive LLM inference introduces persistent capacity constraints that cannot be addressed through provisioning alone. Common degradation approaches rely on service-level mechanisms such as load shedding and circuit breakers, or on feature-level switches (some manually controlled) to preserve availability and quality. While effective at protecting services, such approaches lead to untestable product states and thereby unpredictable product quality. We present HiLO (High Load Optimizer), an automated product-level degradation system designed to handle graceful degradation at scale. HiLO maps observed load to a product state lattice: a small set of pre-validated product states, partially ordered by degradation severity. Dependencies are resolved at design time enabling deterministic and continuous control without requiring runtime dependency discovery. The same abstraction applies unchanged across heterogeneous services, including GPU-intensive deep models, LLMs and their serving layers. At Microsoft, HiLO is deployed in Bing (serving over a billion monthly active users), where it manages on average two traffic surges per week across all datacenters, bounding OneDCG (relevance) drop to under 0.5 points (the operational target) even under sustained load exceeding 2$\times$ baseline peak. HiLO complements existing service-level protections with product-level coordination and makes product quality measurable, testable and predictable.

item.title: Efficient Exact Unlearning for Federated Zeroth-Order Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2610.35211v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Federated zeroth-order optimization (FedZOO) reduces the memory and communication costs of collaborative training for edge intelligence by avoiding backpropagation while communicating only random seeds and scalar coefficients. However, existing methods lack efficient mechanisms for exact unlearning to fully remove the influence of training data when users request deletion. A key insight is that total variation stability of the learning algorithm creates overlap between model distributions before and after data deletion, allowing exact unlearning to reuse computation through coupling. Based on this observation, we jointly design two stable zeroth-order learning algorithms and their corresponding exact-unlearning procedures: \textsc{FedZOO-S} obtains stability through client and mini-batch subsampling, enabling \textsc{FedZOUL-S} to perform efficient unlearning by preserving earlier updates and restarting from the first affected step. \textsc{FedZOO-NS} further combines subsampling with Gaussian noise to increase overlap between update distributions; \textsc{FedZOUL-NS} exploits this overlap through rejection--reflection coupling to reuse affected updates when the coupling is accepted. We prove exact unlearning for both algorithms: the model and saved state have the same joint distribution as retraining with the corresponding learner on retained data. We further establish stability and convergence guarantees for the learning algorithms and derive upper bounds on expected unlearning cost. Experiments demonstrate effective unlearning with competitive model utility and up to $56.1\%$ less cumulative unlearning time than re-optimization. Compared with first-order baselines, our methods reduce communication overhead by up to approximately four orders of magnitude.

item.title: One-Shot Federated Model Editing for Device Dynamics at the Edge
item.description: arXiv:2610.35212v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Standard federated learning (FL) requires persistent device connectivity across multiple communication rounds, making it unsuitable for dynamic environments such as vehicular networks, where devices frequently join and leave. One-shot FL offers a promising alternative by completing training in a single communication round. However, one-shot FL suffers from model solidification and cannot readily adapt to subsequent client dynamics, including new client contributions and the withdrawal of previous contributions.
